entities.name: Li Gonglin
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Li Gonglin (c. 1049–1106), also known by his style name Boshi and art name Longmian Jushi, was a towering figure in Chinese art and culture during the Northern Song dynasty (960–1127). Celebrated as a scholar-official, antiquarian, and arguably the most influential painter of his era, Li Gonglin redefined the aesthetics of literati painting (wenrenhua). His contributions transcended mere artistic skill, establishing a new paradigm that prioritized intellectual depth, calligraphic brushwork, and scholarly self-expression over the professional craftsmanship prevalent in court academies. Operating within the vibrant intellectual milieu of Kaifeng, he associated with leading minds like Su Shi, Huang Tingjian, and Mi Fu, collectively shaping the cultural zenith of the Northern Song.

Born into a wealthy scholar-official family in Shucheng, Anhui province, Li Gonglin passed the imperial examination in 1070, embarking on a distinguished political career that included positions in the Imperial Secretariat and as a censor. Despite his official duties, his true passion lay in collecting and studying ancient artifacts, particularly bronzes and jades, and in painting. He pioneered the "baimiao" (plain line) technique for figure painting, eschewing color to emphasize the expressive power of the ink line, drawing inspiration from Tang dynasty masters like Wu Daozi. His oeuvre spanned diverse subjects, from Buddhist and Daoist figures to landscapes, horses, and genre scenes, meticulously rendered with a refined, calligraphic hand. His most famous works include the 'Five Tribute Horses' scroll and 'Classic of Filial Piety,' both exemplifying his mastery of detailed observation and linear precision.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Li Gonglin's pioneering work in literati painting, particularly his 'baimiao' technique, profoundly shaped Chinese art, establishing new aesthetic values for scholar-artists for centuries. His influence is evident in the trajectory of painting styles through the Yuan, Ming, and Qing dynasties.
